about: A check of each bridge against the Berean Standard Bible text, the OpenBible.info cross-references (data/evidence.json) and the way the New Testament uses the Old. Written with AI assistance as suggestions for the editor. link: quotation | allusion | theme. reading: prophecy | typology | promise | parallel. strength: strong | moderate | weak. verdict and issues are editorial (keep | revise | reconsider) and are not shown in the reading layout. keyOt/keyNt are exact BSB phrases, keyOtPl/keyNtPl exact UBG phrases, highlighted in the reader.

issues: labelled 'Typological Foreshadowing', but the bridge reads Genesis 3:15 as a prediction, not a type
no NT text quotes Genesis 3:15; 'born of a woman' (Galatians 4:4) is a common idiom for being human
Revelation 12:5 mainly echoes Psalm 2:9 (iron scepter); Revelation 12:9, 17 and Romans 16:20 echo Genesis 3:15 more clearly
'heel wound = the Cross' is traditional interpretation, not stated in the NT
p1.note: No New Testament writer quotes Genesis 3:15, so the link rests on echoes: Romans 16:20 promises that God will soon crush Satan under believers' feet, and Revelation 12:9, 17 calls the dragon 'that ancient serpent' and has him make war on 'the rest of her children', using the same Greek word for offspring as the Greek Old Testament in Genesis 3:15. Reading the verse as the 'first gospel' of Christ's victory is an ancient and widespread Christian interpretation, not something the New Testament states outright.

Odczytywanie tego wersetu jako pierwszej zapowiedzi Ewangelii o zwycięstwie Chrystusa to starożytna i powszechna interpretacja chrześcijańska, a nie coś, co Nowy Testament mówi wprost.

issues: minor: author line says Paul, but Acts 3:25 is Peter's sermon (recorded by Luke)
p2.note: Peter quotes God's promise to Abraham almost word for word in Acts 3:25 ('Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed'), and in Galatians 3:16 Paul argues that the promises speak of one 'seed', who is Christ. So the New Testament makes this link itself; Paul's wording 'and to your seed' echoes several of Abraham's promises (for example Genesis 13:15 and 17:8), of which 22:18 is one.

Nowy Testament sam więc tworzy to powiązanie; sformułowanie Pawła „I twemu potomkowi” nawiązuje do kilku obietnic danych Abrahamowi (np. Rodzaju 13:15 i 17:8), a 22:18 jest tylko jedną z nich.

issues: Revelation 5:5's 'Lion of the tribe of Judah' echoes Genesis 49:9; widen the OT reference to 49:9-10
NT never quotes 49:10 or mentions Shiloh, so 'Direct Prophecy' overstates the link
'Shiloh' is a disputed word; 'He to whom it belongs' is one possible reading, stated as fact
Luke 3:33 only shows Judah in Jesus' family line; it does not refer to the scepter promise
p3.note: The New Testament never quotes Genesis 49:10 or mentions Shiloh. Revelation 5:5 calls Jesus 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah', echoing the lion image in Jacob's blessing of Judah (Genesis 49:9), and Luke 3:33 traces the family line of Jesus back to Judah. Jewish and Christian interpreters have long read the scepter promise as pointing to the Messiah, but the meaning of Shiloh is uncertain.

Objawienie 5:5 mówi o Jezusie: „zwyciężył lew z pokolenia Judy”, co nawiązuje do obrazu lwa w błogosławieństwie Jakuba dla Judy (Rodzaju 49:9), a Łukasza 3:33 wywodzi ród Jezusa od Judy. Żydowscy i chrześcijańscy komentatorzy od dawna odczytują obietnicę berła jako zapowiedź Mesjasza, ale znaczenie słowa Szylo jest niepewne.

issues: Matthew never quotes Numbers 24:17 or says the star fulfils it; 'Direct Prophecy' overstates an echo
claim that Balaam's oracle was kept in Eastern wisdom traditions and drew the Magi is speculation, not in the text
p4.note: Matthew does not quote Numbers 24:17 or say that the star fulfils it, though he quotes other prophecies in the same chapter, so the link is an echo: Balaam foresaw a star and a scepter (images of a king), and the Magi saw the star of the newborn 'King of the Jews'. When Jesus calls Himself 'the bright Morning Star' (Revelation 22:16), that too may recall the oracle, which Jewish and Christian readers have long taken as pointing to the Messiah.

Również słowa Jezusa z Objawienia 22:16, że jest „jasną gwiazdą poranną”, mogą przywoływać tę wyrocznię, którą Żydzi i chrześcijanie od dawna odnoszą do Mesjasza.

issues: in Ruth 4:14-15 the 'kinsman-redeemer' is most naturally the newborn Obed; Boaz's act of redemption is in Ruth 4:1-10
explanation merges two laws: buying back family land (Leviticus 25) and levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25, a relative marrying a childless widow); no law required 'buying back a bride'
Boaz as a type of Christ is a traditional reading; no NT text makes it, and Galatians 4:4-5 does not mention Ruth or Boaz
minor: author line omits Paul (Galatians 4:4-5)
p5.note: Matthew 1:5-6 traces the line Boaz–Obed–Jesse–David, matching Ruth 4:17, so the family link is explicit. In Ruth, Boaz acts as kinsman-redeemer by buying Elimelech's land and marrying Ruth (Ruth 4:9-10), and the redeemer praised in Ruth 4:14-15 is most naturally the newborn Obed. Seeing Boaz as a picture of Christ the Redeemer is a long-standing Christian reading, but no New Testament text makes it; Galatians 4:4-5 speaks of redemption without mentioning Ruth or Boaz.
p5.notePl: Mateusza 1:5-6 prowadzi linię Booz–Obed–Jesse–Dawid, zgodną z Rut 4:17, więc związek rodowy jest wyraźny. W Księdze Rut Booz działa jako krewny-odkupiciel, gdy nabywa ziemię Elimelecha i bierze Rut za żonę (Rut 4:9-10), a krewnym wysławianym w Rut 4:14-15 jest najpewniej nowo narodzony Obed. Dostrzeganie w Boozie obrazu Chrystusa Odkupiciela to dawna chrześcijańska interpretacja, ale żaden tekst Nowego Testamentu jej nie podaje; Galacjan 4:4-5 mówi o odkupieniu, nie wspominając Rut ani Booza.

issues: OT reference is only 1 Samuel 2:10, but Mary's song parallels 2:1-8 most closely; widen to 1 Samuel 2:1-10
Luke echoes rather than quotes Hannah ('directly mirror' overstates it); 'horn of salvation' also recalls Psalm 18:2
p6.note: Luke never quotes Hannah, but Mary's song closely follows the pattern of her prayer: God humbles the proud, lifts the lowly and feeds the hungry (compare 1 Samuel 2:4-8 with Luke 1:51-53). Zechariah's 'horn of salvation' in the house of David picks up Hannah's last line, where God will 'exalt the horn of His anointed' ('horn' is a biblical picture of strength), and also recalls Psalm 18:2. The echo is widely recognised, but it is an allusion, not a quotation.
p6.notePl: Łukasz nigdy nie cytuje Anny, ale pieśń Marii wyraźnie idzie za wzorem jej modlitwy: Bóg poniża pysznych, wywyższa pokornych i nasyca głodnych (porównaj 1 Samuela 2:4-8 z Łukasza 1:51-53). W pieśni Zachariasza „róg zbawienia” w domu Dawida nawiązuje do ostatniego wersetu modlitwy Anny, gdzie Pan „wywyższy róg swego pomazańca” („róg” to biblijny obraz siły), a także przypomina Psalm 18:2. To echo jest powszechnie uznawane, ale jest to aluzja, a nie cytat.

p6.keyNt: He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David
p6.keyNtPl: I wzbudził nam róg zbawienia w domu Dawida, swego sługi

issues: Gabriel echoes 2 Samuel 7 (throne, son, endless kingdom) but does not quote it 'directly'; the word-for-word quotation is Hebrews 1:5
minor: author line names only Luke; Hebrews 1:5 comes from Hebrews (author unnamed)
p7.note: Hebrews 1:5 quotes God's promise to David word for word: 'I will be His Father, and He will be My Son'. Gabriel's announcement in Luke 1:32-33 does not quote 2 Samuel 7 but clearly echoes it: Son of the Most High, the throne of David, a kingdom that will never end. In its first setting the promise concerned David's son Solomon, who built the temple; the NT reads its 'forever' as fulfilled in Jesus.
p7.notePl: List do Hebrajczyków 1:5 dosłownie cytuje Bożą obietnicę daną Dawidowi: „Ja będę mu Ojcem, a on będzie mi Synem”. Zwiastowanie Gabriela w Łukasza 1:32-33 nie cytuje 2 Samuela 7, ale wyraźnie do niego nawiązuje: Syn Najwyższego, tron Dawida, królestwo bez końca. W pierwotnym kontekście obietnica dotyczyła syna Dawida, Salomona, który zbudował świątynię; Nowy Testament odczytuje jej „na wieki” jako wypełnione w Jezusie.

p8.note: Matthew says all this took place 'to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet' and quotes Isaiah 7:14 almost word for word, so the New Testament makes the link itself. In Isaiah the sign also addressed King Ahaz's own crisis (Isaiah 7:16), and the Hebrew word almah means a young woman of marriageable age, while the Greek translation Matthew follows says 'virgin'; Matthew presents the birth of Jesus as the sign's fullest meaning.

U Izajasza znak dotyczył też ówczesnego kryzysu króla Achaza (Izajasza 7:16), a hebrajskie słowo alma oznacza młodą kobietę w wieku zamążpójścia, podczas gdy grecki przekład, za którym idzie Mateusz, mówi „dziewica”; Mateusz przedstawia narodzenie Jezusa jako najpełniejsze znaczenie tego znaku.

p9.note: No New Testament writer quotes Isaiah 9:6-7, so the link is an echo rather than a cited prophecy. Gabriel's promise of 'the throne of His father David' and a kingdom that 'will never end' (Luke 1:32-33) recalls Isaiah 9:7, and Luke 2:11 places the Savior's birth in the city of David. Matthew 4:14-16 quotes the opening of this same prophecy (Isaiah 9:1-2) as fulfilled in Jesus, which supports reading the chapter as messianic (about the coming Messiah).
p9.notePl: Żaden autor Nowego Testamentu nie cytuje Izajasza 9:6-7, więc jest to echo, a nie przytoczone proroctwo. Obietnica Gabriela, że Jezus otrzyma „tron jego ojca Dawida”, a „jego królestwu nie będzie końca” (Łukasza 1:32-33), przywołuje Izajasza 9:7, a Łukasza 2:11 umieszcza narodziny Zbawiciela w mieście Dawida. Mateusza 4:14-16 przytacza początek tego samego proroctwa (Izajasza 9:1-2) jako wypełniony w Jezusie, co wspiera mesjańskie odczytanie całego rozdziału (jako zapowiedzi Mesjasza).

p10.note: Paul introduces the words with 'Isaiah says' and quotes Isaiah 11:10 in its ancient Greek translation (the Septuagint), where the Root of Jesse 'will arise to rule over the Gentiles' rather than stand as a banner for the peoples. Matthew 3:16 does not cite Isaiah, but the Spirit coming to rest on Jesus at His baptism is widely seen as an echo of 11:2, where the Spirit rests on the shoot of Jesse.

Ewangelia Mateusza 3:16 nie powołuje się na Izajasza, ale Duch zstępujący na Jezusa przy chrzcie jest powszechnie uznawany za echo wersetu 11:2, gdzie Duch Pana spoczywa na gałązce z pnia Jessego.

p12.note: Matthew says that 'what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled' and quotes Jeremiah 31:15 almost word for word. In Jeremiah, Rachel (one of Israel's ancestral mothers) weeps at Ramah for her descendants taken into exile, not for a future massacre, so Matthew is best read as pointing to a repeated pattern: bitter grief just before God's promised rescue (Jeremiah 31:16-17).
p12.notePl: Mateusz pisze: „Wtedy wypełniło się to, co zostało powiedziane przez proroka Jeremiasza”, i niemal dosłownie cytuje Jeremiasza 31:15. U Jeremiasza Rachel (jedna z matek rodu Izraela) opłakuje w Rama potomków uprowadzonych na wygnanie, a nie przyszłą rzeź, więc Mateusz najpewniej wskazuje na powtarzający się wzorzec: gorzki żal tuż przed obiecanym przez Boga ocaleniem (Jeremiasza 31:16-17).

issues: in Hebrew poetry 'the wicked' and 'a rich man' may be parallel terms, so the contrast between a criminal's grave and a rich man's tomb is debated

issues: Hebrews 4 never cites the Sabbath command: it builds its 'Sabbath rest' on God's own rest at creation (Genesis 2:2, quoted in Hebrews 4:4) and on Psalm 95, so 'Hebrews 4 reads that rest forward' would be more exact as 'reads God's seventh-day rest forward'
Colossians 2:16-17, the plainest NT statement ('a shadow of the things to come'), carries the explanation and the basis line but is missing from the NT reference; consider adding it
Matthew 11:28's 'rest' is not Sabbath language (Matthew places it just before the Sabbath disputes of 12:1-14); present it as a thematic companion, not a Sabbath text
p78.note: Hebrews 4:9 describes the rest still awaiting God's people with a Sabbath word ('a Sabbath rest', Greek sabbatismos) and ties it to God's own seventh-day rest (Hebrews 4:4, quoting Genesis 2:2), while Colossians 2:16-17 calls Sabbaths 'a shadow of the things to come'. So the New Testament itself reads the Sabbath as pointing forward, though it never quotes Leviticus 23:3; Matthew 11:28's promise of rest is a thematic companion rather than Sabbath language.
p78.notePl: List do Hebrajczyków 4:9 opisuje odpoczynek, który wciąż czeka lud Boży, słowem związanym z szabatem (gr. sabbatismos, czyli odpoczynek szabatu), i łączy go z odpoczynkiem samego Boga siódmego dnia (Hebrajczyków 4:4, cytat z Rodzaju 2:2), a List do Kolosan 2:16-17 mówi o szabatach i świętach: „Są to cienie rzeczy przyszłych”. issues: John 1:14's 'made His dwelling' (skēnoō) mainly recalls the tabernacle where God's glory dwelt (Exodus 25:8; 40:34-35; compare 33:18; 34:6); skēnē also names the feast's booths in the Greek Old Testament, but John 1:14 does not point to the feast. Present that link as a reading and soften the basis line's 'John 1:14 uses its word' (e.g. 'John 1:14 and Revelation 21:3 use the Greek word for a tent, skēnē, found in the feast's Greek name')

Revelation 21:3 echoes Leviticus 26:11-12 and Ezekiel 37:27 ('My dwelling place will be with them'); the clearer Tabernacles imagery is Revelation 7:9-17 (palm branches, 'spread His tabernacle over them', 'springs of living water'). 'Revelation closes with the same words' is also loose: 21:3 belongs to the closing vision and shares the word family

John 7:38's 'as the Scripture has said' quotes none of this bridge's OT verses; a likely source is Zechariah 14:8 ('living water will flow out from Jerusalem', in the same chapter as 14:16); consider adding it, and John 7:2, which names the feast, to the references
'Christians read its full meaning as still ahead' generalises; write 'many Christians'
p84.note: John sets Jesus' call to 'come to Me and drink' on the last day of this very feast (John 7:2, 37), so the New Testament itself places Him at Tabernacles. The 'dwelling' words in John 1:14 and Revelation 21:3 come from the Greek word for a tent (skēnē), which the Greek Old Testament also uses for the feast's booths, but they mainly recall the tabernacle where God's glory dwelt; reading them as this feast's fulfilment is a widely shared interpretation, not something the texts say.
p84.notePl: Jan sam umieszcza wezwanie Jezusa „niech przyjdzie do mnie i pije” w ostatnim dniu tego właśnie święta (Jana 7:2, 37), więc Nowy Testament wprost wiąże Jezusa ze Świętem Namiotów. Słowa o mieszkaniu w Jana 1:14 i Objawieniu 21:3 pochodzą od greckiego słowa oznaczającego namiot (skēnē), którym grecki przekład Starego Testamentu nazywa też szałasy tego święta, ale przywołują przede wszystkim przybytek, w którym mieszkała chwała Boża; odczytywanie ich jako wypełnienia tego święta to rozpowszechniona interpretacja, a nie stwierdzenie tekstów.
